extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals and prospective contributors submitting articles to PRSA's Strategies & Tactics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing and submitting feature/how-to/case-study columns to PRSA's Strategies & Tactics, including topical focus, length, style, accuracy, submission format, and copyright expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: We’re interested in articles that: explain new trends in public relations; discuss new technologies that are changing the way that professionals practice public relations; interview exceptional communications practitioners; convey timely news analysis of issues impacting the profession; analyze case studies of successful PR campaigns with measurable outcomes; reflect the growth and change in crucial areas of professional development in the form of how-to pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lively, easy-to-read format
rubrics_metrics.description: All columns must be written in a lively, easy-to-read format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style guidance below (active voice, strong verbs, varied sentence structure) supports this requirement. Editors decide final word count.

rubrics_metrics.name: How-to pieces: focus on execution steps
rubrics_metrics.description: For the how-to angle, topics should focus on how professionals can best execute a tactical skill; place emphasis on the steps required to successfully complete a typical PR task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles may relate to real-life events and should use anecdotes and examples to place advice in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anecdotes and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles may relate to real-life events, using anecdotes and examples to place the advice in a meaningful context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes should illustrate measurable impact or concrete application of the advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributor voice and opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors may interject their personal opinions based on professional experiences and expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal opinions should be grounded in professional experience and clear to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length for how-to articles
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of articles can vary from 600–1,000 words, but the editorial team will decide the final word count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length for senior-level / case studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategies & Tactics seeks articles of specific relevance to senior-level professionals and executives, including case studies. The length of these articles is usually 1,000–1,200 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pieces should relate to real-life events with anecdotes and examples illustrating measurable impact on strategic organizational goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Write in active voice to make writing clear, succinct and more colorful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Don’t say 'There was a presentation given by Matt.' Say: 'Matt gave a presentation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong, active verbs and vivid descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use strong, active verbs and vivid descriptors rather than generic terms like 'good' or 'nice'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete descriptive detail over vague praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary your word choice and use synonyms whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid repetition and monotonous phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary sentence structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary your sentence structure; provide a mix of simple, compound and complex sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing sentence structures improves readability and flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés and tired phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than settle for clichés and tired phrases, seek original images and descriptive adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Don’t say 'He has cold feet.' Say: 'He is timid.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t use blocks of quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use blocks of quotes; instead, weave them into a narrative and place them in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate quoted material so it supports the surrounding analysis or instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize thoughts and use subheadings
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize your thoughts — and use subheadings or section breaks if you need help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put related ideas together, transition smoothly, and avoid jumping back and forth between thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain non-common knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't assume that the reader knows everything; clearly explain or identify anything that may not be common knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute all quotes and sources and identify speakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute all quotes and sources and always identify the speaker properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each quotation is clearly sourced and the individual's role/title is provided when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make references clear (pronoun clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure that references are clear. (If you write 'it,' then make sure that the audience will understand what 'it' refers to.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement (grammar): company is singular
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of agreement. (Refer to a company as 'it,' not 'they,' because 'company' does not take the plural form.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep your audience in mind when writing. Remember who your readers are — and that you are trying to make communications pros better, smarter and more connected through all stages of their career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor examples, tone, and assumed knowledge to PR professionals at the target career stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite surveys and statistics precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the proper name of the survey, who conducted it and the release date when you cite a survey or statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include full attribution so readers can assess source credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite books fully
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the year of publication and the publisher when you reference a book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational but professional tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to write in a conversational tone, but remember to be professional too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance accessibility with professional standards expected by PRSA readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parallel structure in lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parallel structure in your writing. When you use bullet points or list items in a series, construct phrases similarly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Use 'playing tennis, exercising, coloring' not 'playing tennis, exercise, coloring.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow AP style
rubrics_metrics.description: Style — Strategies & Tactics follows AP style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to AP style rules for punctuation, capitalization, numbers, titles, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy — We rely on authors to ensure the veracity of their statements. The writer must double-check names, confirm spellings, provide accurate job titles and include institutions responsible for, and dates of, any research cited in columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are responsible for factual correctness and completeness of attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial prerogative — The editors reserve the right to edit stories for content and style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may change content and style as needed; contributors should expect editorial revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity of submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusivity — We assume that any article submitted to Strategies & Tactics is offered exclusively and that substantially similar articles will not be published elsewhere simultaneously without our knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bios and headshot requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Bios — Include biographical information for the author (nearly 30 to 40 words) at the end of columns, along with a high-resolution headshot (300 dpi or greater).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise bio and a professional-quality image that meets resolution requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission format and method
rubrics_metrics.description: Format — Please submit all articles via email, attached as a Word document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright transfer and originality warranty
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright Information: The contributor conveys all rights, title and interest, including any statutory copyright together with the right to secure renewals and extensions of such copyright throughout the world to Strategies & Tactics. The contributor warrants that this work is original except for such excerpts from copyrighted works as may be included either with the written permission of the copyright owners or as 'fair use' under the Copyright Act, and that the work does not invade the privacy or rights of publicity of any person or organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With permission, contributors may reprint an article in PDF form and online for educational purposes only with specified credit language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response timeframe / no guarantee of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting an article does not guarantee its publication. Due to the high volume of submissions received, we cannot guarantee a response to all queries. An editorial team member will likely respond within a week to 10 days of submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor-in-chief reserves the right to exercise absolute discretion when selecting articles for publication.
